findings.explanation: google_apigee_instance.main is a bare singleton — no count, no for_each — so the module produces exactly one runtime instance in var.location. Apigee X supports multiple instances under one organization precisely so that runtime traffic survives a regional outage, but a caller cannot get that here: instantiating the module twice would try to create a second google_apigee_organization, and Apigee allows only one organization per project. The result is that any consumer wanting multi-region Apigee has to fork the module rather than configure it. Nothing deterministic can flag this because every individual resource is well-formed; it is the module's shape that forecloses HA.
findings.remediation: Replace the singleton instance and attachment with for_each over a map of region -> { ip_range, kms_key_name }, keeping google_apigee_organization.main singular. Existing single-region callers keep working if the map defaults to one entry built from var.location.
findings.title: Module structurally caps the deployment at one Apigee runtime instance in one region, and the one-org-per-project limit means a second module instance cannot supply HA

findings.explanation: retention is unset, so the organization is created with DELETION_RETENTION_UNSPECIFIED — a seven-day soft delete. Because Apigee permits one organization per project, a terraform destroy followed by a re-apply fails for a full week with the project still holding a soft-deleted org, and there is no Terraform-side escape hatch. That is a severe iteration trap for a module whose own example is a disposable eval stack, and it is invisible to a rules engine because the failure comes from an absent attribute interacting with a service-side quota rather than from anything in the config.
findings.remediation: Add a nullable variable retention (validated against DELETION_RETENTION_UNSPECIFIED / MINIMUM) and set it on google_apigee_organization.main, so eval and CI stacks can choose MINIMUM (24h) while production keeps the seven-day default.
findings.title: google_apigee_organization sets no retention, so a destroy leaves the project unusable for Apigee for seven days

findings.explanation: README.md line 38 warns that 'An Apigee organization ... takes 30-45 minutes to provision, so plan timeouts accordingly', but neither google_apigee_organization.main nor google_apigee_instance.main carries a timeouts block, and the module exposes no variable to set one. A caller who hits the slow end of that range, or a slower region, has no way to extend the provider default without forking — and a timed-out apply on a half-created Apigee org leaves state and reality diverged on a resource that cannot simply be re-created.
findings.remediation: Add a timeouts { create = var.create_timeout, delete = var.delete_timeout } block to google_apigee_organization.main and google_apigee_instance.main, defaulting to "60m" so current behaviour is preserved.
findings.title: No timeouts block on the organization or instance, though the module's own README documents 30-45 minute provisioning

findings.explanation: var.billing_type defaults to PAYG, which bills per gateway node-hour, yet the environment has no node_config block and the module offers no variable for one. Autoscaling therefore runs between Apigee's own defaults, so a caller cannot lower min_node_count for a dev environment or cap max_node_count to bound spend. Combined with the PAYG default this means the module's out-of-the-box configuration starts billable nodes that the consumer has no lever to reduce.
findings.remediation: Add nullable variables min_node_count and max_node_count and emit a dynamic node_config block on google_apigee_environment.main when either is set, leaving current behaviour when both are null.
findings.title: google_apigee_environment sets no node_config, so a PAYG organization bills at Apigee's default node floor with no caller control

findings.explanation: Every other tunable in this module — analytics_region, location, billing_type, environment_name, description — is a validated variable, but deployment_type = "PROXY" and api_proxy_type = "PROGRAMMABLE" are literals. Both attributes have real alternatives in provider google 7.46.0 (ARCHIVE and CONFIGURABLE), and both are ForceNew, so a consumer who needs an archive-deployment or configurable-proxy environment must fork rather than configure. This is an internal-consistency gap in the module's own parameterisation, not something any single-resource rule can see.
findings.remediation: Add variables deployment_type (default "PROXY", validated one of PROXY/ARCHIVE/CONFIGURABLE-compatible values) and api_proxy_type (default "PROGRAMMABLE", validated PROGRAMMABLE/CONFIGURABLE), matching the validation style already used by var.billing_type.
findings.title: deployment_type and api_proxy_type are hardcoded on the environment while every other Apigee attribute in the module is a variable

findings.explanation: README.md line 33 says private services access needs 'a `/16` (or larger) reserved range', but variables.tf line 66 describes var.ip_range as 'a /22 and a /28 separated by a comma', and example/examplea/google_compute_global_address.apigee.tf now reserves a /21. Three documents in one repo state three different sizes for the same range, so a consumer following the README over-reserves 65,536 addresses on a peered VPC. Prose is entirely outside the deterministic engine's reach.
findings.fix:
services access with a `/21` reserved range (a /22 plus a /28 per runtime
instance; use a /20 to leave room for a second instance) before the
findings.remediation: Update README.md line 33 to state the actual requirement — a /22 plus a /28 per runtime instance, so a /21 covers one instance and a /20 leaves headroom for two — and reference the example's prefix_length rather than restating a number.
findings.title: README states the peered range must be a /16 or larger, contradicting the example's /21 and the module's own /22 + /28 documentation

findings.explanation: The destroy target runs `terraform destroy -force`. That flag was deprecated in 0.11 and removed in 0.15, while terraform.tf requires >= 1.5.0 — so `make destroy` fails immediately with an unknown-flag error on every version this module supports. Given an Apigee org's seven-day soft delete (see HOLDEN_BP_002), a broken teardown path is the one that hurts most. Makefiles are outside holden's Terraform target entirely.
findings.remediation: Replace -force with -auto-approve on line 43 of example/examplea/Makefile.
findings.title: Example Makefile destroy target uses terraform destroy -force, a flag removed in Terraform 0.15

findings.explanation: README.md line 12 says the module 'Exercises holden's google_apigee_organization and google_apigee_instance policies', and .holden.yaml configures scan roots — yet the valid target invokes checkov (with an --external-checks-dir ../../checkov that does not exist in this repo), terrascan and a docker-pulled kics, and never calls holden. The repo's declared primary linter is the one thing its own lint target skips.
findings.remediation: Add `-holden scan . --targets terraform` to the valid target, and drop the checkov --external-checks-dir flag since ../../checkov does not exist here.
findings.title: Example Makefile valid target runs checkov, terrascan and kics but not holden, in a repo whose stated purpose is exercising holden policies

findings.explanation: The condition `can(regex("^[0-9./,]+$", var.ip_range))` passes on "1", "...", "////" and "999.999.999.999/99", so the validation gives false assurance while catching essentially nothing. Every other variable in this file uses a genuinely constraining check — instance_name has an anchored name regex, billing_type uses contains() against an explicit set — so this is the outlier. An invalid ip_range surfaces as an apply-time API error on a resource that takes 30-45 minutes to provision.
findings.remediation: Anchor the regex to real CIDR shape, e.g. `can(regex("^([0-9]{1,3}\\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}/[0-9]{1,2}(,([0-9]{1,3}\\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}/[0-9]{1,2})?$", var.ip_range))`, or use cidrhost() inside can() to let Terraform itself parse each comma-separated element.
findings.title: var.ip_range validation regex accepts any string of digits, dots, slashes and commas — including values that are not CIDRs at all

findings.explanation: "europe-west2" appears literally in google_kms_key_ring.apigee.tf line 3 and twice in module.apigee.tf (analytics_region and location), with no local or variable tying them together — yet the KMS key ring location and the Apigee instance location must match for the CMEK to be usable. Meanwhile provider.google.tf sets only default_labels, so project and region come from ambient GOOGLE_PROJECT / ADC state, making the example's behaviour depend on the operator's shell. Re-pointing the example at another region means finding four unlinked strings and hoping none was missed.
findings.fix_note: Example provider sets region from local.region but not project: wiring project from data.google_project.current creates a provider/data-source cycle, so project still comes from ambient GOOGLE_PROJECT/ADC.
findings.remediation: Introduce a `locals { region = "europe-west2" }` in example/examplea and reference local.region from the key ring, analytics_region and location; add project and region to the provider block so the example does not depend on ambient environment.
findings.title: europe-west2 is hardcoded in four places across the example and the provider block pins neither project nor region

suggested_policies.rationale: google_apigee_environment has zero policy coverage today — coverage_by_type lists nothing for it, and holden's only Apigee rules are HLD_GCP_428 (instance disk CMEK), HLD_GCP_429 (org runtime DB CMEK) and the newly added HLD_GCP_526 (org API consumer data CMEK). node_config is the environment's only cost lever: for PAYG and SUBSCRIPTION organizations Apigee bills per gateway node-hour, and with node_config absent autoscaling runs between Apigee's own defaults with no declared ceiling. The check is a plain not_null on one attribute of one resource type and fires correctly on any Terraform declaring an Apigee environment, so it is a genuine deterministic rule rather than a judgment call.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_GCP_528
name: Apigee environments should declare a node_config to bound gateway node autoscaling
principle: cost
severity: LOW
rationale: |
  For PAYG and SUBSCRIPTION Apigee organizations, gateway nodes are billed per
  node-hour. When google_apigee_environment omits node_config, autoscaling runs
  between Apigee's own default minimum and maximum node counts, so the
  configuration declares no floor a dev environment can be lowered to and no
  ceiling that bounds spend during a traffic spike. Declaring node_config makes
  both ends of that range explicit and reviewable in the Terraform itself.
remediation: |
  ```hcl
  resource "google_apigee_environment" "main" {
    org_id = google_apigee_organization.main.id
    name   = "eval"

    node_config {
      min_node_count = 2
      max_node_count = 5
    }
  }
  ```
resources:
  google_apigee_environment:
    path: node_config
    not_null: true
